=== guarantees
# Guarantees

This is what walq promises to the services built on it. A behaviour that breaks one of these is a bug, whatever the code comments say. "Crash" here means a process being killed at any instant. "Power loss" means the machine stopping, with anything not yet synced to disk gone.

## Durability

**G1. An acknowledged call survives.** Once a call that changes the queue has returned, its effect survives any crash or power loss.

**G2. A queue always reopens after a crash.** No crash or power loss, at any point in any operation, leaves a queue that needs manual repair.

**G3. Unacknowledged work leaves no trace of damage.** A write that was cut off is not a reason to refuse the log, and it must not affect anything written afterwards.

**G4. Damage to acknowledged data is reported, never repaired away.** If bytes that held acknowledged records are damaged, walq raises `CorruptLogError` with the offset, and leaves the file as it found it. It must not drop acknowledged records to keep going.

**G5. Size is not a risk.** Logs and records of any size within the format's limits work the same way.

## Jobs

**G6. One owner at a time.** A job has at most one valid lease at any moment, across all processes on the host. Each attempt has its own token, and a token is never issued twice for a job, for as long as the job exists.

**G7. A live worker keeps its job.** A worker that keeps heartbeating does not lose its job to lease expiry, whichever process runs the reaper.

**G8. Old leases have no power.** A worker holding a token that is no longer current cannot change the job.

**G9. Retries keep their schedule.** A retry's due time is fixed when the failure happens. Restarts and compaction do not move it, and every process sees the same time. Attempt counts carry through too, so backoff keeps growing and `maxAttempts` holds.

**G10. Keys are remembered for their whole time to live.** Within `idempotencyTtlMs`, a repeated key returns the original job and its outcome, even if the job itself has since been pruned, however many compactions and restarts have happened, and whichever processes race on it.

## Compaction

**G11. Compaction changes nothing you can observe,** apart from finished jobs past `retainCompletedMs` going away. All other job fields come through unchanged.

**G12. Compaction can fail safely at any moment.** If it's killed or blocked at any step, the queue keeps working and a later compaction can succeed. Other processes on the host, including operators' tools with the log open, are a normal part of life on Windows hosts and must not cause lasting failure.

**G13. Every process follows.** After any process compacts, every other process continues correctly, with no restart, whatever the sizes of the old and new logs.

**G14. Automatic compaction keeps the log bounded without dominating the work.** Its cost per write stays small even when the live state is larger than `compactAfterBytes`.

## Workers

**G15.** See RFC 007 for what happens when workers die.
=== crash-testing
# Crash testing

A queue that's only tested when nothing goes wrong tells you little. walq has two tools for testing the other case. Both are part of the project, and other teams' test suites depend on them, so keep the names and meanings on this page stable.

## Failpoints

A failpoint is a named place in the code. Arm one with environment variables, and a process dies or stops there:

```
WALQ_FAILPOINTS="wal.mid-append#complete=kill@2,claim.before-lock=pause"
WALQ_FAILPOINT_DIR=C:\some\folder
```

A rule is `name[#type]=action[@nth]`.

- `kill` terminates the process with no cleanup, on the `nth` time the point is reached (default the first). It first writes `<name>.hit` to the marker folder and doesn't fire again while that file exists, so a restarted worker doesn't die at the same place forever.
- `pause` writes `<name>.paused` and blocks until `<name>.release` appears. A `#` in the name becomes `.` in the file names.
- `#type` limits the rule to one record type, for the `wal.*` points.

Within one process, `onFailpoint(name, callback)` runs a callback at the point instead, so that a test can run something else at exactly that moment. `clearFailpoints()` removes all callbacks.

|---|---|---|
| `enqueue.before-lock` | `enqueue()` is about to take the lock to add the job | No |
| `claim.before-lock` | `claim()` is about to take the lock to lease a job | No |
| `reap.before-lock` | `reapExpired()` is about to take the lock to return jobs | No |
| `complete.before-lock` | `complete()` is about to take the lock | No |
| `wal.before-append` | Records are encoded and nothing is written yet | Yes |
| `wal.mid-append` | Half of the bytes have been written | Yes |
| `wal.after-write` | All bytes are written, not yet synced | Yes |

                                  â–¼
                     data/queue/wal.log        the log
                     data/queue/queue.lock     the cross-process lock
```

## Shared log, no server

Every process that opens a queue directory holds its own copy of the state, built by replaying the log. Nobody is in charge. A process that wants to do something:

1. takes the lock (`lock.mjs`);
2. reads whatever other processes appended since last time, and applies it (`Store.catchUp`);
3. decides, appends, and syncs;
4. releases the lock.

Time spent holding the lock is short, because job handlers run outside it.

## Modules

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `queue.mjs` | The public API. Turns calls into records |
| `store.mjs` | Lock + catch-up + append. Owns the in-memory state and its log offset |
| `state.mjs` | The reducer: `applyRecord(state, record)` |
| `snapshot.mjs`, `retention.mjs` | What a compacted log keeps |
| `compactor.mjs` | Rewrites the log |
| `wal.mjs`, `frame.mjs`, `crc32.mjs` | The file and its encoding |
| `fsops.mjs` | File operations, real or power-loss model |
| `lock.mjs` | The cross-process mutex |
| `lease.mjs`, `backoff.mjs`, `idempotency.mjs` | Pure rules |
| `failpoints.mjs` | Named crash and pause points |
| `metrics.mjs`, `logger.mjs`, `inspect.mjs`, `cli.mjs` | Operations |
| `worker/pool.mjs` | Starts and replaces worker processes, runs the reaper |
| `worker/child.mjs` | Entry point of a worker process |
| `worker/runner.mjs` | The claim, run, report loop |
| `worker/registry.mjs` | Loads handlers, enforces handler timeouts |
| `worker/protocol.mjs` | Messages between pool and workers |

## Synchronous on purpose

All queue calls are synchronous. A call never interleaves with another call in the same process, which keeps reasoning about one process simple. The hard part is the other processes.

## Who runs the reaper

`WorkerPool` calls `reapExpired()` on a timer, in the parent process. Anyone may call it; it is safe to have several. Pools can share a queue directory, and so can processes that only enqueue.
=== operations
# Operations

## Files

A queue directory holds `wal.log` and `queue.lock`. Temp files named `wal.log.*` can appear during compaction. Don't edit any of these by hand while the queue is in use.

## Logging

Silent by default. Set `WALQ_LOG=info` (or `debug`, `warn`, `error`) for JSON lines on stderr.

## metrics()

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `byType` | Job counts by type and status |
| `dueNow` | Ready jobs whose time has come |
| `delayed` | Ready jobs waiting for their time |
| `retriedJobs` | Jobs on their second attempt or later |
| `oldestReadyAgeMs` | How long the longest-waiting due job has waited |
| `nextLeaseExpiryMs` | Time until the next lease deadline, or null |
| `activeWorkers` | Distinct workers holding leases |
| `idempotencyKeys` | Keys currently remembered |
| `jobsEverEnqueued` | Total since the queue was created |
| `generation`, `logBytes` | The log |
| `tornTailsDropped` | Incomplete tails this process has dealt with |
| `lastCompactionError` | Why the last automatic compaction failed, or null |

## Tools

```
node src/cli.mjs inspect <dir>        every record in the log
node src/cli.mjs stats <dir>          job counts
node src/cli.mjs metrics <dir>        the table above
node src/cli.mjs compact <dir>        compact now
node src/cli.mjs tail <dir>           follow the log as it grows
node src/cli.mjs requeue <dir> <id>   give a dead job new attempts
node src/cli.mjs cancel <dir> <id>    stop a job
```

`inspect` takes no lock and changes nothing, so it's safe at any time. `tail` keeps the log open for as long as it runs.

## Sizing

Each write takes the lock and syncs, so throughput follows the disk's sync latency. The lock is shared by all processes on a queue, so a handful of workers per queue is the expected size. Run more queues rather than more workers.

## Upgrades

The log format is stable. Stop the workers, deploy, and start them again. Older logs open without any conversion.

  "description": "A small durable job queue backed by a write-ahead log. No runtime dependencies.",

    "node": ">=24"

    "test": "node --test test/*.mjs",
    "stress": "node scripts/stress.mjs"

```

|---|---|---|
| `enqueue.before-lock` | `enqueue()` is about to take the lock to add the job | No |
| `claim.before-lock` | `claim()` is about to take the lock to lease a job | No |
| `reap.before-lock` | `reapExpired()` is about to take the lock to return jobs | No |
| `complete.before-lock` | `complete()` is about to take the lock | No |
| `wal.before-append` | Records are encoded and nothing is written yet | Yes |
| `wal.mid-append` | Half of the bytes have been written | Yes |
| `wal.after-write` | All bytes are written, not yet synced | Yes |
| `wal.after-fsync` | The records are durable, and the call has not returned | Yes |

| `compact.before-rename` | The temp file is about to replace the log | Yes |
| `compact.after-rename` | The temp file has replaced the log | Yes |
| `job.before-handler` | A worker holds a lease and has not called the handler | No |
| `job.after-handler` | The handler has returned, and nothing is recorded yet | No |
| `job.after-complete` | `complete()` has returned | No |

## The power-loss model

Killing a process doesn't lose anything the operating system has already accepted, so a kill on its own can't show what happens when the power goes. Set `WALQ_SIMULATE_POWER_LOSS=1` and `fsops.mjs` models the page cache: written bytes stay in the process until that file is synced, and only then reach the disk. `npm run stress` runs real workers through rounds of contention, kills and compaction, and checks the results. It takes about 90 seconds and prints every run and every record, so send it to a file if you only want the summary. Failures are often intermittent. Use `--seed` for a different mix.
=== wal-format
# Log format

The format is a compatibility contract. Logs already on production hosts must stay readable, so changes must be additive.

## File

`wal.log` is a header followed by frames. All integers are little-endian.

### Header (20 bytes)

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 4 | Magic, ASCII `WALQ` |
| 4 | 2 | Format version, currently 1 |
| 6 | 2 | Flags, zero |
| 8 | 4 | Generation |
| 12 | 4 | Reserved, zero |
| 16 | 4 | CRC-32 of bytes 0 to 15 |

A new log starts at generation 1. Each compaction adds one.

### Frame (10 bytes + payload)

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | Magic, bytes `AD FB` |
| 2 | 4 | Payload length |
| 6 | 4 | CRC-32 over the length field and then the payload |
| 10 | n | Payload: one record, as UTF-8 JSON |

The payload limit is 64 MiB. Valid UTF-8 cannot contain the byte `FB`.

## Records

Every record has `t`, its type, and `at`, the writer's clock when it was written (a snapshot's `at` is when it was built).

| `t` | Fields | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `enqueue` | `id, type, payload, key, priority, maxAttempts, availableAt, at` | A new job, `ready` |
| `claim` | `id, worker, fence, leaseUntil, at` | Job `leased`, attempts + 1, token = `fence` |
| `heartbeat` | `id, fence, leaseUntil, at` | Lease deadline moves |
| `complete` | `id, fence, result, at` | Job `done` |
| `fail` | `id, fence, error, delayMs, at` | Job `ready` again, after a delay |
| `expire` | `id, fence, error, delayMs, at` | Same, because the lease ran out |
| `dead` | `id, fence, error, at` | Job `dead` |
| `cancel` | `id, fence, error, at` | Job `cancelled` |
| `requeue` | `id, at` | Dead job `ready` again, attempts back to 0 |
| `snapshot` | `at, seq, jobs, ...` | Replaces all state. Always the first record of a compacted log |

A reader ignores record types it doesn't know. Older logs may lack newer fields: `priority` counts as 0, and an older snapshot may lack `attempts`, `fence` and `idem`.

Job ids are `j<n>`, where `n` is the count of jobs ever enqueued, and are never reused.
=== rfc-007-exactly-once-completion
# RFC 007: Exactly-once completion

**Status:** accepted, not implemented.

## Problem

Execution is at-least-once, and that's fine: a job's handler can run more than once. Completion is the part consumers rely on. Today a consumer can't tell a first completion from a repeat, can't look up a result by job id in any stable way, and a worker's death is only noticed when its lease runs out, which can be minutes.

## What we want

**A job commits at most once. A worker killed before the commit leads to the job running again. A commit that has been recorded never leads to the job running again,** whatever happens afterwards, in any process.

The commit point is the moment the `complete` record is durable. There's no state in between.

## API

### complete(id, token, result)

Returns a receipt:

```js
{ id, outcome, token, result, completedAt, completionSeq }
```

- First commit with the current token: `outcome: 'committed'`.
- Repeat with the token that committed, including after a restart or a compaction: `outcome: 'already-committed'`. The receipt carries the stored `result`, `completedAt` and `completionSeq`. The result passed in is ignored, and nothing is written to the log.
- Any other token: `StaleLeaseError`, and nothing changes.
- A job that has been pruned: `UnknownJobError`.

A lease past its deadline can still commit, as long as nobody has acted on it. Its token is still current until a reaper, a reclaim or a cancel says otherwise.

### getResult(id)

- A finished job: `{ id, status: 'done', result, token, attempts, completedAt, completionSeq }`.
- Any other job: `{ id, status }`.
- Not known (never existed, or pruned): `null`.

Results survive restarts and compaction until `retainCompletedMs` has passed.

### completions({ after = 0, limit })

The retained commits in commit order: `[{ seq, id, token, result, completedAt }]`, with `seq > after`. Numbers start at 1, go up by one with each commit, and carry on across restarts and compaction, including when older entries have been pruned. Readers keep their own position.

### reclaimWorker(workerId, { reason })

Gives up every lease held by a worker that's known to be dead, at once, without waiting for expiry. Returns `[{ id, status }]`.

- The job is runnable straight away, with no backoff: `status: 'ready'`. The new record type is `release`, with fields `id, fence, error, at`. `error` is the reason, and it becomes the job's `lastError`.
- The attempt counts. If attempts have run out, the job goes `dead` with a `dead` record.
- Jobs the worker already committed aren't touched and produce no record.
- The old token is stale from this moment.

## Workers and pools

**`WorkerPool` reclaims a dead worker's leases** as soon as it sees the worker exit, and starts a replacement. A job shouldn't have to wait for its lease when the pool already knows its worker is gone. A reclaim must only ever affect the worker that died.

**A worker doesn't give up on a finished job.** Once a handler has returned, its outcome is worth more than anything else the worker could be doing. If recording it fails because the queue is busy or the disk hiccups, the worker keeps trying until the outcome is recorded or it learns it has been fenced. It reports `job-fenced` in that case. It shouldn't start another job in the meantime.

A worker that's been fenced stops there. Its result is discarded.

## Crash table

| The worker dies... | What happens |
|---|---|
| Before the handler runs | Job runs again |
| During the handler | Job runs again |
| After the handler, before `complete` | Job runs again |
| Part way through writing `complete` | Job runs again |
| After the `complete` record is durable, before `complete` returns | Job does not run again |
| After `complete` returns | Job does not run again |

The same table holds if the machine loses power instead, and if a compaction was running.

## Compatibility

No format change except the new record type. Older logs have no `completionSeq` on finished jobs. Those jobs aren't listed by `completions()`, and numbering starts after them.

=== compaction
# Compaction

The log only grows, so from time to time it's replaced by a shorter one that says the same thing: a new header with the next generation, and one `snapshot` record.

## When

- `compact()` runs it on request.
- After any write, automatically, when the log has passed `compactAfterBytes`.

A failed automatic compaction doesn't fail the call that triggered it, because that call has already committed. `stats().lastCompactionError` shows the last failure.

## How

Compaction runs under the queue lock, after catching up, so the state it writes is complete.

1. Build the snapshot from the current state, dropping finished jobs past `retainCompletedMs`.
2. Write the header and snapshot to `wal.log.compact`.
3. Rename it over `wal.log`.
4. Sync, and rebuild this process's state from the snapshot.

## What the snapshot holds

The jobs that are kept, and the counters the log needs to carry on. See [guarantees.md](guarantees.md), G10 and G11.

## Other processes

A process that was reading the old log finds a different file next time it catches up, and has to start again from the new one.
=== leases-and-retries
# Leases and retries

## Leases

`claim()` gives a job to a worker until `leaseUntil`, and hands back a `token`. The token goes on every later call about that attempt. A lease has expired once the clock reaches its deadline.

A worker running a long job calls `heartbeat()`. `JobRunner` does this on a timer, every `leaseMs / 3` by default.

Anyone can call `reapExpired()`. It returns expired jobs to the queue with a backoff, or sends them to `dead` when attempts have run out. An expired lease counts as a used attempt.

## Tokens

The token is the job's `fence`, which goes up by one with each claim. A call with a token that isn't current throws `StaleLeaseError`.

## Backoff

After an attempt fails, the job is due again after:

```
delay = min(maxMs, baseMs * factor ^ (attempts - 1))
```

With `jitter` above zero, the delay is reduced by up to that fraction. The reduction is derived from the job id and the attempt number, so that it's reproducible.

## Attempts

`attempts` counts claims. When an attempt ends in failure or expiry with `attempts >= maxAttempts`, the job goes `dead`. `requeueDead()` sets attempts back to zero and makes the job due now.

## Clocks

All processes are on one host and read the same system clock, so clock skew between processes isn't handled.
# API

Everything is exported from `src/index.mjs`. The names and shapes on this page are a contract with the services that use walq.

## openQueue(dir, options)

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `leaseMs` | 30 000 | Default lease length |
| `lockTimeoutMs` | 10 000 | How long a call waits for the lock before `LockTimeoutError` |
| `compactAfterBytes` | 4 MiB | Compact automatically past this size. `0` turns it off |
| `retainCompletedMs` | 24 h | How long finished jobs stay in the log after they finish |
| `idempotencyTtlMs` | 7 d | How long a key is remembered, from when the job was enqueued |
| `maxAttempts` | 5 | Default attempts per job |
| `backoff` | `{ baseMs: 1000, factor: 2, maxMs: 60000, jitter: 0 }` | Retry schedule |
| `clock` | system clock | Anything with `now()`. Tests use `ManualClock` |

## Queue

**`enqueue(type, payload, { key, delayMs, maxAttempts, priority })`** returns `{ id, status, deduped }`. With a remembered `key` it also returns the existing job's `result` and `deduped: true`, and creates nothing.

**`enqueueMany([{ type, payload, options }])`** adds a batch under one lock and one sync. A crash can leave a prefix of the batch behind.

**`claim(worker, { leaseMs, types })`** returns `{ id, type, payload, attempt, token, leaseUntil }` or `null`. Among due jobs, higher `priority` goes first, then the job due longest, then the oldest. `token` identifies this attempt.

**`heartbeat(id, token, { leaseMs })`** returns `{ leaseUntil }`. Throws `StaleLeaseError` if the lease is no longer yours.

**`complete(id, token, result)`** records the result. Throws `StaleLeaseError` if the lease is no longer yours. RFC 007 changes what this returns.

**`fail(id, token, error)`** returns `{ id, status, retryAt }`. The job goes back to `ready` with a backoff, or to `dead` when attempts run out.

**`reapExpired()`** returns jobs whose lease had run out to the queue, and returns `[{ id, status, retryAt }]`.

**`cancel(id, { reason })`** stops a job that is `ready` or `leased`. Returns `{ id, status, changed }`. A worker holding the job loses its lease.

**`requeueDead(id)`** gives a dead job a new set of attempts, runnable now. Returns `{ id, status }`. Throws `InvalidTransitionError` if the job is not dead.

**`getJob(id)`** returns a copy of the job or `null`. **`listJobs()`** returns copies of all jobs in the log. **`stats()`** returns counts by status, plus `total`, `generation`, `logBytes`, `tornTailsDropped` and `lastCompactionError`. **`metrics()`** is described in [operations.md](operations.md).

**`compact()`** rewrites the log now and returns `{ generation, bytesBefore, bytesAfter, jobs }`. If it throws, the queue is still usable and nothing is lost.

**`close()`** marks this instance closed.

## Job fields

`id`, `type`, `payload`, `key`, `priority`, `status` (`ready`, `leased`, `done`, `dead`, `cancelled`), `attempts`, `fence` (the current token), `maxAttempts`, `availableAt`, `lease` (`{ worker, fence, until }` or null), `result`, `lastError`, `enqueuedAt`, `completedAt`, `seq`.

## WorkerPool

```js
new WorkerPool({ dir, handlers, size, leaseMs, heartbeatMs, pollMs, reapMs, types, env, queue, maxRespawns })
```

`handlers` is the path of a handlers module. `queue` is the options object for `openQueue` in the workers and the pool, so it must be JSON-serialisable. `env` adds environment variables for the workers. `types` limits which job types the pool's workers take.

- `start()` starts the workers.
- `drain({ timeoutMs })` resolves when no job is `ready` or `leased`, and rejects when that takes too long.
- `stop()` stops the workers and waits for them to go.

The pool is an `EventEmitter`. `message` carries worker events (`kind` is one of `ready`, `job-started`, `job-completed`, `job-failed`, `job-fenced`, `worker-error`), `exit` fires when a worker exits, and `stderr` and `error-event` report problems.

## Errors

`WalqError` is the base class. `CorruptLogError` has an `offset`. Also `StaleLeaseError`, `UnknownJobError`, `LockTimeoutError`, `InvalidTransitionError`, `ConfigError`, `QueueClosedError`.

## Other exports

`computeBackoff(attempts, policy, salt)`, `ManualClock`, `SystemClock`, `JobRunner`, `inspectLog(dir)`, `describeRecord(record)`, `onFailpoint`, `clearFailpoints`, `hit`.

# Compaction

The log only grows, so from time to time it's replaced by a shorter one that says the same thing: a new header with the next generation, and one `snapshot` record (followed by `snapshot-more` records if the state is too big for one frame).

## When

- `compact()` runs it on request.
- After any write, automatically, when the log has passed `compactAfterBytes` and has at least doubled since the last snapshot, so a live state larger than the threshold is not rewritten on every write. After a failure the next attempt waits for another `compactAfterBytes` of growth.

A failed automatic compaction doesn't fail the call that triggered it, because that call has already committed. `stats().lastCompactionError` shows the last failure.

## How

Compaction runs under the queue lock, after catching up, so the state it writes is complete.

1. Build the snapshot from the current state, dropping finished jobs past `retainCompletedMs`.
2. Write the header and snapshot to `wal.log.compact` (an earlier leftover is overwritten) and sync it.
3. Rename it over `wal.log`. If another process has `wal.log` open and the platform refuses (`EPERM`, `EACCES`, `EBUSY`), the old log is renamed to `wal.log.old.<generation>` first, the new one renamed in, and the old one removed.
4. Sync, and rebuild this process's state from the snapshot.

Opening a queue (under the lock) finishes any compaction that was cut short: if `wal.log` is missing the newest `wal.log.old.*` is put back, and leftovers are removed.

## What the snapshot holds

The jobs that are kept in full (including `priority`, `attempts` and `fence`), the idempotency keys still within their time to live, and the counters the log needs to carry on. See [guarantees.md](guarantees.md), G10 and G11.

## Other processes

A process that was reading the old log sees a different generation next time it catches up, and starts again from the new one, whatever the sizes of the two files.

Opening a queue (under the lock) finishes any compaction that was cut short: if `wal.log` is missing the newest `wal.log.old.*` is put back, and leftovers are removed.

## What the snapshot holds

The jobs that are kept in full (including `priority`, `attempts` and `fence`), the idempotency keys still within their time to live, and the counters the log needs to carry on. See [guarantees.md](guarantees.md), G10 and G11.

## Other processes

A process that was reading the old log sees a different generation next time it catches up, and starts again from the new one, whatever the sizes of the two files.

text: Last check: the full suite, and that the doc edits rendered correctly.

I fixed the root causes I found and implemented RFC 007. I couldn't run `npm run stress` or any real-process test here, so none of this has been checked with real kills.

This sandbox blocks spawning child processes (`spawn EPERM`), and `.git` is read-only. Six existing tests need to spawn processes and fail here for that reason: the 5 worker-pool tests and the kill-during-append test in `test/recovery.mjs`. Please run `npm run stress` several times, with different `--seed` values, on a real host before trusting this.

I ran everything else in-process with `node --test --test-isolation=none test/*.mjs`, using the power-loss model and failpoint callbacks. 69 tests pass. Of my 20 new durability tests, 15 fail against the original source. The other 5 are guards for behaviour that already held, and the 13 RFC tests in `test/completion.mjs` have no old-source run to compare against.

**Incident root causes**
- **Won't open after power loss:** a torn tail was reported but never cut off, so later writes landed behind it. `wal.log` is now cut off at the torn tail when it is found. Damage with a valid frame after it still raises `CorruptLogError` with the offset and leaves the file untouched (G4). `src/frame.mjs`, `src/store.mjs`
- **0-byte log after compaction:** the new log was renamed into place without being synced. It is now synced first. A new log's first creation is also synced. `src/compactor.mjs`, `src/wal.mjs`
- **Jobs lost on a big log:** the 1 MiB scan chunk treated a record cut by the chunk edge as a torn tail, so the rest was silently dropped. Scans now read on until a frame fits. This is my best explanation for the large-queue loss, but I have no reproduction.
- **Compaction EEXIST:** a leftover `wal.log.compact` blocked every later compaction, so I removed the exclusive create. Opening a queue also finishes an interrupted compaction.
- **Compaction EPERM:** the rename now moves the old log aside to `wal.log.old.<generation>` when another process has it open. `walq tail` also no longer holds the log open. I couldn't test Windows's behaviour with a handle opened without share-delete.

**Other guarantee breaks**
- **Double runs:** heartbeats lived only in the worker's memory, so another process's reaper expired live jobs. They are now log records. Claim also re-picks the job under the lock.
- **Stale idempotency key:** snapshots dropped keys. They are now stored with a TTL, and the lookup runs under the lock.
- **Retry timing:** replay used the clock at replay time instead of the record's `at`. Snapshots dropped `priority`, `attempts` and `fence`, and `requeue` reset the fence.
- **Compaction detection:** other processes now notice a compaction by its generation, not by file size. Automatic compaction no longer rewrites a large live state on every write.
- **Large logs:** a state too big for one frame is split across `snapshot-more` records, and an oversized record is refused when written.

**RFC 007**
- `complete()` now returns a receipt. It is durable before it returns and is idempotent on a repeat with the same token.
- I added `getResult`, `completions` and `reclaimWorker`, plus the `release` record.
- The pool reclaims a dead worker's leases when it sees the worker exit.
- The runner keeps trying to record a finished job.
- Failpoint names and the public API are unchanged apart from RFC 007's additions. Docs, CHANGELOG and version (0.5.0) are updated.

**Caveats**
- **Compatibility:** old logs open without conversion. A log containing `release` or `snapshot-more` records can't be read by older code.
- **Heartbeat cost:** heartbeats append unsynced records, so heartbeat traffic adds log growth.
- **Cancelled jobs:** they are never pruned by retention (unchanged from before). That is probably a leak, but I left it.
- **Original test failure:** the original "bad checksum last record" test failed before my changes and passes now.
- **New test files:** `test/durability.mjs`, `test/completion.mjs` and `test/helpers/crash.mjs` are new. No existing test was weakened.
